DISCOVER_AMAZON.TITLE: The Amazon is not just a rainforest; it is a living organism that breathes and beats.
DISCOVER_AMAZON.TEXT_1: Imagine a place where life doesn't just exist—it overflows. The Amazon is far more than a forest: it is the planet's lungs and one of the great engines that sustain our climate. Every breath you take, part of that air is born here, among millions of trees that regulate the Earth's temperature and store vast amounts of carbon.
DISCOVER_AMAZON.TEXT_2: Spanning over 7 million square kilometers, this is the largest continuous natural paradise on Earth. A territory where biodiversity reaches staggering numbers: nearly one in every ten known species calls these lands home. To grasp its magnitude, consider this surprising fact: a single hectare of the Amazon rainforest can harbor more tree species than the entirety of Europe.
DISCOVER_AMAZON.TEXT_3: The Amazon River, the mightiest in the world, carries roughly 20% of the fresh water reaching the oceans, weaving together jungles, wildlife, and cultures for millennia. Everything in this ecosystem is bound by a balance as powerful as it is delicate.
DISCOVER_AMAZON.TEXT_4: This is a true natural sanctuary. Every insect, every medicinal plant, and every species yet to be discovered holds secrets that modern science is still striving to understand. Here, nature does not simply reveal itself: it manifests.
DISCOVER_AMAZON.TEXT_5: To walk through the jungle is to encounter untouched wilderness in its purest state. From the jaguar's roar to the whisper of the rivers, from the treetops to the pulsing ground beneath your feet, everything serves as a reminder of one essential truth: we are not separate from nature; we are part of it.
DISCOVER_AMAZON.TEXT_6: Protecting the Amazon means protecting the balance of our planet. And ultimately, our own future.

JAGUAR.DESCRIPTION: The supreme predator of the Amazon, the jaguar is the largest feline in the Americas and the third largest in the world. With its distinctive golden coat decorated with black rosettes, this nocturnal hunter dominates its territory with powerful bites capable of piercing skulls and shells. An excellent swimmer, it hunts on both land and in water, being fundamental to the balance of the Amazonian ecosystem.

TAPIR.DESCRIPTION: The gardener of the forest, the Brazilian tapir is one of the largest herbivorous mammals in South America. With its distinctive flexible trunk and robust body, this distant relative of rhinoceroses and horses disperses seeds through the forest, being crucial for forest regeneration. A shy and mainly nocturnal animal, it prefers areas near water where it can submerge to escape predators.

PECARI.DESCRIPTION: The social architect of the jungle, the white-lipped peccary lives in massive herds of up to 300 individuals that move noisily through the forest. Recognizable by its characteristic white lip, this omnivore plays an essential role in seed dispersal and invertebrate control. Their large groups can significantly modify the understory, creating gaps that benefit other species.

JAGUAR.TITLE: Jaguar
JAGUAR.POEM: "Obsidian eyes that see in the dark, a golden breath that roams the thicket, the indomitable heartbeat of the jungle's core."
JAGUAR.BODY_1: The Panthera onca, absolute sovereign of the Amazonian shadows, is the largest feline in the Americas. Its coat, a masterpiece of camouflage with rosettes that mimic the play of light and shadow in the primary forest, envelops a body of pure power and agility.
JAGUAR.BODY_2: As an alpha predator, the jaguar plays a vital role in regulating the populations of other species, maintaining the balance of biodiversity. Its bite, the strongest among all large felines, is capable of piercing even the toughest shells.
JAGUAR.BODY_3: Unlike other felines, the jaguar is an exceptional swimmer that patrols riverbanks in search of caimans and capybaras. Its presence is an indicator of the ecosystem's health; where the jaguar roars, the jungle pulses with ancestral strength.
JAGUAR.BODY_4: In the worldview of Amazonian peoples, the jaguar is a guardian of wisdom and nocturnal power. It is the spirit that protects the earth's secrets, moving with the same elegance and silence as time itself through the Emerald Carpet.

TAPIR.TITLE: Brazilian Tapir
TAPIR.POEM: "A trail of life in the fertile mud, a trunk that caresses the green leaf, the quiet step that sows the eternal forest."
TAPIR.BODY_1: The Tapirus terrestris, affectionately known as the "gardener of the jungle," is the largest land mammal in South America. With its characteristic flexible trunk, an appendage it uses to reach fresh leaves and fruits, the tapir is a distant relative of rhinoceroses and horses.
TAPIR.BODY_2: Its role in the ecosystem is irreplaceable: by consuming a vast diversity of fruits, it disperses seeds over great distances, ensuring the regeneration and vitality of the forest. It is a silent architect that plants the future of the jungle with every step.
TAPIR.BODY_3: Mainly crepuscular and nocturnal in its habits, the tapir is a shy animal that seeks the coolness of water, where it is an excellent swimmer and diver. Its thick skin and robust build allow it to move through dense vegetation with surprising agility.
TAPIR.BODY_4: For the guardians of the jungle, the tapir symbolizes perseverance and connection with the deep earth. Its presence is a reminder of the importance of the slow and steady processes that sustain life in the heart of the Amazon, far from the bustle of the upper canopy.

PECARI.TITLE: White-lipped Peccary
PECARI.POEM: "A thunder of hooves in the leaf litter, a tide of life flowing between the trunks, the collective pulse of the jungle in motion."
PECARI.BODY_1: The Tayassu pecari, or white-lipped peccary, is the social architect of the Amazon rainforest. These relatives of pigs, recognizable by their dark fur and characteristic white lip, live in massive herds that can exceed 300 individuals, creating a collective force that shapes the forest landscape.
PECARI.BODY_2: Their movement through the forest is a seismic event for biodiversity: their trampling and foraging on the ground open gaps in the understory, allowing light to reach new seedlings and regulating populations of invertebrates and small vertebrates.
PECARI.BODY_3: Endowed with a strong sense of hierarchy and communication, peccaries use tactile and olfactory signals to maintain group cohesion. They are brave animals that, together, can face even large predators like the jaguar to protect their young.
PECARI.BODY_4: In the ecology of the Amazon, the peccary represents the power of the collective. Its presence is vital for maintaining the structure and composition of the primary forest, reminding us that even the smallest animals, when acting in harmony, can transform the world they inhabit.
PECARI.VIDEO_TITLE: The Red List, Endangered Species - White-lipped Peccary

BIRDS.TITLE: Amazonian Birds
BIRDS.TOUCAN_BODY_1: Ramphastos vitellinus, a jewel of the Amazonian canopy, is distinguished by its vibrant vitelline-yellow throat and the bluish base of its bill. As an architect of the rainforest, it plays a crucial role as an efficient seed disperser, weaving the threads of biodiversity with every flight through the upper canopy.
BIRDS.TOUCAN_BODY_2: An inhabitant of the Amazon Basin lowlands, its characteristic vocalization pierces the thicket, setting the rhythm of the morning. Its skeletal structure and bill—though massive in appearance—are surprisingly lightweight, allowing it to reach fruits on the thinnest branch tips.
BIRDS.TOUCAN_BODY_3: As a living emblem, the toucan transcends its biological role to become the quintessential symbol of the Amazon. This vast basin serves as the ultimate sanctuary for the Ramphastidae family, sheltering the greatest diversity of toucan species on the planet.
BIRDS.TOUCAN_BODY_4: Its undulating flight—a choreography of rises and falls over the green ocean—guides the eye toward the secrets of the rainforest. Its presence serves as a barometer for forest health, a vibrant note on the staff of life that breathes spirit into the immense emerald carpet.
BIRDS.TOUCAN_QUOTE: "Its robust bill, a master tool for seed dispersal, resonates through the stillness of the Amazonian morning—a vibrant echo within the symphony of the rainforest."
BIRDS.COTINGA_BODY_1: For many ornithologists and explorers, the Spangled Cotinga represents the ultimate aesthetic expression of the Amazon Basin. This passerine is distinguished by a turquoise plumage so vibrant it seems to radiate its own luminescence amidst the forest shadows. What we perceive as color is, in truth, a marvel of biophysics: the blue of its feathers is not derived from pigments but from structural coloration. The microstructures within the feathers refract light such that only the blue spectrum is reflected back to our eyes, creating a "jeweled" visual effect that stands in dramatic contrast to the dense, eternal green of the jungle.
BIRDS.COTINGA_BODY_2: A silent inhabitant of the forest’s highest strata, the cotinga plays a fundamental ecological role as the Amazon's "gardener." As an eminently frugivorous species, it feeds on a vast array of wild fruits, dispersing seeds over great distances after they pass through its digestive tract. This symbiotic relationship ensures the regeneration of botanical species that would otherwise remain confined to the shade of their progenitors. Thus, the bird’s beauty is not a mere ornament, but rather the engine of a natural engineering process that maintains the complex architecture of the ecosystem.
BIRDS.COTINGA_BODY_3: Unlike more vociferous birds such as macaws, the Spangled Cotinga is a master of discretion and mystery. It lacks a complex song, often communicating through subtle mechanical sounds produced by its wings during flight.
BIRDS.COTINGA_QUOTE: "Its presence is a reminder that nature does not always need to shout to impose its majesty."
BIRDS.COTINGA_BODY_4: This natural shyness makes it a rare treasure to behold—an ethereal spirit that favors the safety of the canopy, where the sun strikes with the greatest intensity, allowing its cobalt plumage to shine with full brilliance. Its presence is a reminder that nature does not always need to shout to impose its majesty.
BIRDS.COTINGA_BODY_5: To witness a male perched atop an emergent tree, its deep purple throat contrasting sharply against the turquoise, is to observe a moment of biological transcendence. It is the embodiment of both fragility and resilience; a fragment of the sky that has descended to dwell among the leaves. Its form encapsulates millions of years of evolutionary history, where natural selection has sculpted shapes and hues that defy human imagination, reminding us that life always finds a way to celebrate its own existence through pure art.
BIRDS.COTINGA_BODY_6: However, the persistence of this cerulean shimmer depends entirely on the integrity of its habitat. Habitat fragmentation and the loss of primary forests threaten to extinguish these "spangles" from the treetops. Protecting the cotinga is, in essence, preserving the chromatic palette of a rainforest that serves as the lungs and soul of our planet. Each time a cotinga takes flight, the Amazon sends a message of hope wrapped in sapphire feathers, reminding us of our responsibility to sustain the Earth's visual symphony.
BIRDS.TANGARA_BODY_1: The Paradise Tanager (Tangara chilensis) is, without question, one of the most dazzling living jewels of the Amazon Basin. A member of the Thraupidae family, this small passerine—measuring roughly thirteen centimeters in length—seems to defy the conventional laws of natural sobriety. Its plumage is a vibrant canvas where fluorescent apple-green on the face, electric blue on the breast, and a deep crimson on the rump converge, creating a contrast that feels more like an intentional artistic expression than a mere byproduct of evolution.
BIRDS.TANGARA_BODY_2: An inhabitant of the forest’s highest strata, this bird spends its life within the canopy, that dense green ceiling where sunlight strikes with the greatest intensity. It is there, often at heights exceeding thirty meters, that the Paradise Tanager fulfills its ecological role as an active seed disperser. While its diet is predominantly frugivorous, it also expertly gleans small insects from among the foliage, moving with a frenetic energy that symbolizes the inexhaustible vitality of the tropical rainforest.
BIRDS.TANGARA_BODY_3: From a scientific perspective, its coloration is not merely an aesthetic caprice but a marvel of structural biophysics. Unlike pigments that simply absorb and reflect specific wavelengths, the iridescent blue tones of its breast are the result of the feathers' microscopic structure, which scatters sunlight to create a brilliance that appears almost ethereal.
BIRDS.TANGARA_BODY_4: Its social behavior is equally compelling. The Paradise Tanager is a gregarious species that finds security in collectivity; by integrating into diverse mixed-species flocks, it optimizes foraging efficiency and minimizes predatory risk. Its calls are sharp and rapid—a sort of coded language that maintains flock cohesion as they navigate the vast "ocean of leaves." In this sense, the species is not merely a resident of the Amazon, but a vital musical note in the complex symphony of biodiversity that defines the region.
BIRDS.TANGARA_BODY_5: Ultimately, the Paradise Tanager serves as a silent reminder of its ecosystem's fragility. While its beauty invites poetic contemplation, its survival depends strictly upon the integrity of the primary and secondary forests it calls home. To protect its habitat is to ensure that future generations may still marvel at this "brushstroke of paradise".
BIRDS.TANGARA_QUOTE: "-A masterpiece that, after millions of years of adaptation, continues to soar through the skies of the planet's greatest reservoir of life."

TOUCAN.DESCRIPTION: The Channel-billed Toucan is a living emblem of the Amazon, noted for its vivid yellow throat and the bluish base of its beak. This 'architect of the jungle' is an efficient seed disperser that inhabits the upper canopy, where its characteristic call sets the rhythm of the tropical morning.

COTINGA.DESCRIPTION: The Spangled Cotinga is the ultimate aesthetic expression of the Amazon. Its vibrant turquoise-blue plumage has a luminescence of its own thanks to its structural coloration. A master of mystery and 'gardener' of the forest, it silently disperses seeds from the highest levels of the canopy.

TANGARA.DESCRIPTION: The Paradise Tanager is one of the most dazzling living jewels of the basin. With its apple-green face and electric-blue breast, this small gregarious bird defies natural sobriety as it travels the canopy in mixed groups, ensuring vital seed dispersal.

UNA_DE_GATO.TITLE: Cat's Claw
UNA_DE_GATO.DESCRIPTION: Cat's Claw is an Amazonian vine that climbs toward the sun using claw-shaped thorns. Renowned for its oxindole alkaloids, it acts as a powerful natural immunomodulator and broad-spectrum anti-inflammatory. It is, in essence, a biological shield that transmutes the jungle's vitality into medicine, protecting the body's integrity with the tenacity of an ancestral guardian.

SANGRE_DE_GRADO.TITLE: Dragon's Blood
SANGRE_DE_GRADO.DESCRIPTION: Dragon's Blood is an Amazonian tree that, when wounded, bleeds a thick reddish latex of astonishing regenerative capacity. Rich in taspine and proanthocyanidins, this resin acts as a potent natural healing agent and antiseptic, sealing tissues with an instant protective barrier. It is, in essence, a scarlet tear of the jungle that transmutes the tree's pain into medicine, restoring the skin.

AYAHUASCA.TITLE: Ayahuasca
AYAHUASCA.DESCRIPTION: Ayahuasca is the 'vine of the soul,' a master plant and ritual axis for spiritual cleansing and connection with the forest's spirit. Rich in beta-carbolinas, its pharmacology allows for a deep purge and expansion of consciousness. It is a visionary bridge that merges the self with the pulse of the jungle, drawing back the veil of the invisible with millenary wisdom.

UNA_DE_GATO.TITLE: Cat's Claw
UNA_DE_GATO.BODY_1: Uncaria tomentosa, commonly known as cat's claw, is a climbing vine from the Rubiaceae family native to the virgin rainforests of Peru. Its name comes from the curved thorns that grow along the stem, which it uses to attach itself to trees.
UNA_DE_GATO.BODY_2: Globally recognized for its potent oxindole alkaloids, this plant acts as a natural immunomodulator and broad-spectrum anti-inflammatory. Indigenous communities consider it a biological shield that protects the body's integrity.
UNA_DE_GATO.BODY_3: For centuries, the Asháninka and other Amazonian ethnic groups have used the bark and roots to treat various ailments, from joint pain to digestive issues. Today, it is one of the most studied and appreciated medicinal plants in modern phytotherapy.
UNA_DE_GATO.BODY_4: Its presence in the understory is a reminder of the living pharmacy that is the Amazon. Each vine rising toward the sun is a link between the earth and health, a promise of well-being woven into the jungle's wood.
UNA_DE_GATO.POEM: "Its vegetative claws do not wound, but rather sustain life, transmuting the jungle's strength into medicine for the soul and body."
UNA_DE_GATO.VIDEO_TITLE: WHAT IS CAT'S CLAW FOR? WHAT ARE ITS PROPERTIES AND HOW TO TAKE IT?

PROPERTIES_CARDS.TITLE: Pain reduction in osteoarthritis
PROPERTIES_CARDS.DESC: Helps decrease joint pain caused by cartilage wear during movement.
PROPERTIES_CARDS.SOURCE: NIH - National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health.

PROPERTIES_CARDS.TITLE: Immune system modulation
PROPERTIES_CARDS.DESC: Its alkaloids stimulate white blood cells' ability to fight pathogens.

PROPERTIES_CARDS.TITLE: Rheumatoid arthritis relief
PROPERTIES_CARDS.DESC: Used as a complementary treatment to reduce swelling and morning stiffness.

PROPERTIES_CARDS.TITLE: Antioxidant properties and DNA repair
PROPERTIES_CARDS.DESC: Could help cells recover from oxidative damage, though more human trials are needed.

PROPERTIES_CARDS.TITLE: Treatment of digestive issues (gastritis)
PROPERTIES_CARDS.DESC: Common use to cleanse the digestive tract, but clinical evidence is still limited.

UNA_DE_GATO.PROPERTIES_AMAZON_USE: Local inhabitants consume it mainly as a decoction (tea) of the bark. It's used as a general tonic to "clean the blood," treat urinary inflammations, and as a preventative against diseases when feeling weak or exhausted.
UNA_DE_GATO.PROPERTIES_PHARMA_USE: It is a best-seller in the dietary supplement market. It is processed into capsules, liquid extracts, and ointments. Although there are patents on its specific alkaloids, its main use remains as an adjuvant phytopharmaceutical in anti-inflammatory therapies.

SANGRE_DE_GRADO.TITLE: Dragon's Blood
SANGRE_DE_GRADO.BODY_1: Croton lechleri, popularly known as dragon's blood, is a tree from the Euphorbiaceae family that can reach 20 meters in height. Its most distinctive feature is the deep red latex that flows from its bark when wounded.
SANGRE_DE_GRADO.BODY_2: This latex is a jewel of the Amazonian pharmacopeia, rich in taspine and proanthocyanidins. Its ability to accelerate wound healing and act as a powerful natural antiseptic makes it an indispensable element for health in the jungle.
SANGRE_DE_GRADO.BODY_3: Traditionally used to treat ulcers, hemorrhages, and various skin infections, the latex creates an instantaneous protective barrier over the skin, functioning as a "liquid bandage." It is, in essence, a scarlet tear the tree offers to restore life.
SANGRE_DE_GRADO.BODY_4: Dragon's Blood is a symbol of nature's resilience and generosity. Just as the tree heals its own incisions, it teaches us that in the heart of the forest lies the balm for our own wounds, both physical and spiritual.
SANGRE_DE_GRADO.POEM: "A crimson drop that springs from the heart of the wood, sealing skin and destiny with the earth's regenerative strength."
SANGRE_DE_GRADO.VIDEO_TITLE: The medicinal properties of Dragon's Blood | Green Health

PROPERTIES_CARDS.TITLE: Accelerated wound healing
PROPERTIES_CARDS.DESC: The alkaloid taspine stimulates fibroblast migration to rapidly close cuts and burns.

PROPERTIES_CARDS.TITLE: Treatment of HIV-associated diarrhea
PROPERTIES_CARDS.DESC: Its component crofelemer blocks excess water secretion in the intestine.

PROPERTIES_CARDS.TITLE: Antiviral effect against Herpes
PROPERTIES_CARDS.DESC: Applied topically, it reduces the lifespan of herpes simplex lesions.

PROPERTIES_CARDS.TITLE: Protection against gastric ulcers
PROPERTIES_CARDS.DESC: Forms a protective film over the stomach mucosa, aiding regeneration.

PROPERTIES_CARDS.TITLE: Treatment of insect bites
PROPERTIES_CARDS.DESC: Neutralizes bite toxins and reduces inflammation and itching almost immediately.

SANGRE_DE_GRADO.PROPERTIES_AMAZON_USE: It is the "first aid" remedy par excellence. Local inhabitants always carry a vial of the liquid resin. It is applied directly on any cut or insect bite; as it dries, it forms a reddish crust that acts as a natural, waterproof bandage.
SANGRE_DE_GRADO.PROPERTIES_PHARMA_USE: It is the most successful example of a plant transitioning from the jungle to the modern pharmacy. The drug Crofelemer (Mytesi) is an FDA-approved medication extracted directly from this plant, used to treat chronic diarrhea in patients undergoing antiretroviral therapy.

AYAHUASCA.TITLE: Ayahuasca
AYAHUASCA.BODY_1: Banisteriopsis caapi, known as ayahuasca or "vine of the soul," is the preeminent master plant of the Amazon. This giant vine is the base of a sacred brew that has been used for millennia by indigenous peoples for spiritual healing and connection with the cosmos.
AYAHUASCA.BODY_2: Its pharmacology is fascinating: rich in beta-carbolines such as harmine and tetrahydroharmine, it acts by allowing other visionary compounds to be processed by the body. It is, in essence, the key that opens the doors of perception and deep introspection.
AYAHUASCA.BODY_3: More than a drug, ayahuasca is considered a sentient being, a guiding spirit that facilitates the purging of physical and emotional toxins. Ceremonies led by master healers seek to restore the balance between the human being, nature, and the invisible.
AYAHUASCA.BODY_4: Its presence in the jungle structures the spiritual map of the Amazon. It is a living bridge that reminds us of our interconnection with everything that breathes, a mirror that reflects the vastness of the universe within ourselves.
AYAHUASCA.POEM: "The rope that joins heaven and earth, drawing back the veil of the invisible to reveal the eternal symphony of the jungle."
AYAHUASCA.VIDEO_TITLE: Ayahuasca Documentary, "The medicine of the soul"

PROPERTIES_CARDS.TITLE: Treatment of treatment-resistant depression
PROPERTIES_CARDS.DESC: Produces rapid and lasting improvement in depression symptoms that do not respond to conventional drugs.

PROPERTIES_CARDS.TITLE: Therapy for Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD)
PROPERTIES_CARDS.DESC: Facilitates the processing of traumatic memories by allowing a different emotional perspective.

PROPERTIES_CARDS.TITLE: Recovery from substance addiction
PROPERTIES_CARDS.DESC: Helps reduce substance craving in patients with alcohol or cocaine dependency.

PROPERTIES_CARDS.TITLE: Stimulation of neuroplasticity
PROPERTIES_CARDS.DESC: Compounds such as dimethyltryptamine (N,N-DMT) promote the growth of new neurons.

PROPERTIES_CARDS.TITLE: Emotional regulation and self-awareness
PROPERTIES_CARDS.DESC: Improves introspective capacity and emotional acceptance through modification of neural networks.

AYAHUASCA.PROPERTIES_AMAZON_USE: For tribes such as the Shipibo or the Asháninka, it is a sacred medicine. It is not used to "cure" isolated symptoms, but rather to cleanse the spirit, receive guidance from the ancestors, and allow the shaman to diagnose the spiritual root of a physical ailment.
AYAHUASCA.PROPERTIES_PHARMA_USE: It is currently at the center of a psychiatric revolution. Several biotechnology companies (such as ATAI Life Sciences) are conducting clinical trials to synthesize its compounds and create standardized medications that offer the therapeutic benefits without necessarily undergoing the prolonged psychedelic experience.

WAORANI.TITLE: Waorani
WAORANI.SUBTITLE: Waorani Tribe
WAORANI.DESCRIPTION: In the untamed heart of Yasuní, the Waorani stand as one of the last bastions of cultural resistance. Known for their lineage of master hunters and their unique language, Wao Terero, they fight to preserve their balance with the land against external pressures, protecting the freedom of their relatives in voluntary isolation.

PAGE.HERO_BODY_1: In the untamed heart of Yasuní, the Waorani stand as one of the last bastions of cultural resistance in the Amazon basin. Although official history marks them as the last contacted people of Ecuador after their complex missionary encounter in 1958, their lineage harbors an even deeper secret: the existence of the Tagaeri and Taromenane, relatives who have chosen to remain in voluntary isolation to this day, protecting their freedom the deep rainforest.
PAGE.HERO_BODY_2: In the twilight of the forest, the Waorani move with almost spectral agility, asserting themselves as master hunters who dominate the art of stealth. They craft blowguns and curare to hit prey such as the howler monkey high in the canopy with surgical precision, while their pambil-wood spears are reserved for tracking larger ground animals like the collared peccary, symbolizing the strength of a people deeply respectful of every spirit that inhabits their territory.
PAGE.HERO_BODY_3: Their traditional attire is a statement of simplicity and dignity that challenges the outsider's gaze. The Waorani man wears only the komi, a plant-fiber cord tied around the waist securing his organ—a garment symbolizing maturity, protection, and passage into adulthood. In a world that now pressures them with oil drilling and deforestation, the Waorani struggle to preserve this way of life, reminding us that true wealth lies not in our possessions but in the balance we maintain with the earth we tread upon.
PAGE.HERO_BODY_4: Ultimately, the true essence of the Waorani lives within their language, Wao Terero, a "language isolate" with no known relatives worldwide, holding the worldview of a people where humanity and nature are one. They consider themselves the spiritual heirs of the jaguar and the harpy eagle, figures that populate their ancient chants and stories.
PAGE.HERO_QUOTATION: "Spiritual heirs of the jaguar and the harpy eagle, where humanity and nature are one."

VIDEO_SECTION.TITLE: Waorani Territory, in the heart of the Amazon

LANGUAGE.TITLE: Unique Language
LANGUAGE.DESC: They speak Wao Terero, an isolated language completely unrelated to any other language on Earth.

MASTERS.TITLE: Masters of the Jungle
MASTERS.DESC: They possess extraordinary botanical and zoological knowledge, identifying hundreds of plants and animals.

HUNTERS.TITLE: Silent Hunters
HUNTERS.DESC: Experts in using blowguns with curare-laced darts to hunt down prey without alerting the surroundings.

HOUSING.TITLE: Collective Housing
HOUSING.DESC: They live in communal homes called 'nanicabo', housing multiple generations of the same extended family.

RESISTANCE.TITLE: Resistance and Territory
RESISTANCE.DESC: They maintain a historic defense of their territory against external threats and mining pressures.

LANGUAGE_SECTION.TITLE: Wao Terero
LANGUAGE_SECTION.HERO_TEXT: The language of the Waorani nationality is an isolated linguistic enigma, wholly unrelated to any other language family in the world. It dictates their worldview, wherein the word itself, their territory (ome), and family (nanicabo) decide who is a "true human" (wao) and who is a stranger or visitor (cowode).

MODULE_1.CARD_1_DESC: A system of memory preservation through the original spoken word. Through chants and stories, millennia of myths, botany, and survival strategies have been passed down intact among families.
MODULE_1.CARD_2_DESC: Initiated in the 1950s by the SIL. While elders (pikenani) protect and honor their orality, younger generations employ a bilingual system based on the Latin alphabet as a form of cultural mediation.

MODULE_2.SUBTITLE: An economy of sounds allowing highly fluid and precise auditory communication through the dense forest.

C2.TITLE: Waorani
C2.REL: Shared ethnic identity unified by language and common origin.

C3.TITLE: Huarani
C3.REL: Latent hostility, competition, or potential alliances.

C4.TITLE: Cowode
C4.REL: Originally the cannibal enemy. Today: settlers, oil workers, missionaries, or visitors.

MODULE_4.SUBTITLE: The ömë is not just a weapon; it relies on engineering, empirical physics, and botany.

ITEMS.I1: Ömë: The primary blowgun, carved from the palm tree Iriartea deltoidea.
ITEMS.I2: Nënë: Darts meticulously whittled from chonta wood.
ITEMS.I3: Omi: Curare; a muscle-paralyzing neurotoxin extracted from various Strychnos sap mixtures.
ITEMS.I4: Wii: Kapok cotton, collected to ensure a proper air-pressure seal.
ITEMS.I5: Bëi: The sacred jawbone of a piranha, the main tool for notching and sharpening darts.
ITEMS.I6: Nënë tewe: A protective woven bamboo quiver (Dowe) to survive the humid environment.

CARDS.C1_DESC: Divided into Times of War (scarcity, defensive mobility) and Times of Peace (harvests, feasts, and alliances within the nanicabo longhouse).
CARDS.C2_DESC: The forest knows no drawn Western borders; it is demarcated entirely by sacred memories laid by forefathers and subtle sounds carried by the wind.

TIMELINE.T1_DESC: External violence, enslavement, and defense of sovereignty.
TIMELINE.T2_DESC: A period of forced settlement and restructuring into the nuclear family model, abandoning ancient terms.
TIMELINE.T3_DESC: Introduction of currency-based economies and the environmental struggle in indigenous reserves against exploitation.
TIMELINE.T4_DESC: Full exercise of rights to resist bioprospecting and unify territories through organizations like the "Waorani Observatory."

LANGUAGE_SECTION.CONCLUSION:
In a world where danger encroaches upon their natural stillness, as long as Wao Terero breathes... the Waorani will confidently define themselves as the "true human beings." They will sustain their ancestral authority over their origin myths, botany, and lives, deep within the unfettered heart of the Amazon Basin.

Their spoken word embodies their grandest temple and their most resilient armor.

SHUAR.TITLE: Shuar
SHUAR.SUBTITLE: People of the Sacred Waterfalls
SHUAR.DESCRIPTION: The Shuar are historically known as one of the few peoples that neither the Inca Empire nor the conquerors managed to subordinate, leading one of the most successful rebellions against the Spanish crown. Their mystical ritual of shrunken heads, or "Tzantza", was not a mere trophy, but a ceremony to capture the enemy's spirit and restore spiritual balance.

COFAN.TITLE: Cofán
COFAN.SUBTITLE: Jaguar Men
COFAN.DESCRIPTION: The Cofán are an ancestral people of the northern Ecuadorian Amazon, known as the "jaguar men" and speakers of A'ingae, a unique language in the world. Their culture centers on spiritual connection with the jungle through Yagé and a historic defense of their territory against oil exploitation. As guardians of biodiversity, they have achieved key legal victories to protect their sacred lands, maintaining a vital balance between their ancient traditions and modern resistance.

KAYAPO.TITLE: Kayapó
KAYAPO.SUBTITLE: Guardians of the Forest
KAYAPO.DESCRIPTION: The identity of the Kayapó people is articulated through a worldview where the social and spiritual converge in ancestral rites of profound symbolic significance. For this community, belonging begins with the Bemp, a naming ritual that grants social wealth by linking the child to their lineage, and is consolidated through rites of passage that mark maturity and collective responsibility. Their close connection to the Amazonian environment is manifested in the Jaguar Ritual, a totem of strength and jungle protection, while the mask dances (Kokô) act as a communication channel to summon spirits and mythical heroes, thus preserving a cultural heritage deeply connected to its roots and social evolution.

PAGE.HERO_BODY_1: The Mebêngôkre nation, known to the world as the Kayapó, are not merely inhabitants of the jungle, but its fiercest architects and defenders. Calling themselves the "People of the Water Well", their identity is woven with the Iriri and Xingu rivers, in a territory spanning millions of hectares of rainforest and savanna. For them, survival is not passive; it is a continuous resistance fusing ancestral memory with a vanguard vision of protecting life on Earth.
PAGE.HERO_BODY_2: The circular design of their villages mirrors the cosmos, with each home arranged in harmony with the sun and moon's movement. At the absolute heart of this structure beats the "Warriors' House" (ngà-be), the nucleus of political and ritual life where the community's destiny is forged. This spatial arrangement honors a vital balance: while the center is the male domain of assembly and oratory, the outer ring is the sanctuary of women, who under a matrilocal system maintain lineage continuity and domestic stability.
PAGE.HERO_BODY_3: For a Mebêngôkre, the body is a canvas of wisdom and language is an art form. They pride themselves on being those who "speak beautifully" (Kaben mei), valuing oratory as the ultimate expression of status and humanity. This pursuit of beauty extends to their skin, adorned with geometric patterns in black jenipapo and red urucum mimicking the perfection of jungle animals and insects. Every stroke and feather in their headdresses declares an indestructible connection to the spirit dwelling in all things.
PAGE.HERO_BODY_4: Their relationship with nature eclipses mere subsistence; it is purposeful ecological engineering. Through the creation of apêtê or "forest islands", the Kayapó have proven that human hands can enrich biodiversity rather than destroy it, transporting nutrients and seeds to forge oases of medicine and food in the open savanna. This ancestral knowledge, identifying hundreds of medicinal plants and managing soil with millimeter precision, establishes their culture as a global model for sustainable bioeconomy.
PAGE.HERO_BODY_5: The contemporary history of the Kayapó chronicles their invincibility against the threats of unbridled progress. Led by legendary figures like Chief Raoni Metuktire and female Chief Tuíre Kayapó, they have carried the Amazon's cry to international forums, transforming their warrior culture into a political activism protecting the global climate. Their legacy reminds us that to protect the rainforest is to protect the very root of human existence.
PAGE.HERO_QUOTATION: "Guardians of the Amazon's Pulse, where true wealth lies in the capacity to live in symbiosis with the natural world."

LIFECYCLE_SECTION.DESC: The life of the Mebêngôkre is a constant flow of ceremonies that mark the growth of the soul and the connection with the spiritual plane, celebrating each individual's transition within the great community.

BIOECONOMY_SECTION.DESC: Through a respectful model of resource use, the Kayapó generate well-being for their communities without compromising the integrity of the jungle, becoming benchmarks of the standing-forest economy.

MEHINAKU.TITLE: Mehinaku
MEHINAKU.SUBTITLE: Children of the Sun Path
MEHINAKU.DESCRIPTION: The Mehinaku are an essential pillar of the Upper Xingu, known for their circular villages that reflect their cosmology and a social life of radical transparency. As masters in managing the public and the sacred, they preserve their Arawak identity through ancestral rituals and a deep connection with the celestial cycle.

PAGE.HERO_BODY_1: The Mehinaku, belonging to the Arawak linguistic family, form an essential pillar of the multi-ethnic complex of the Upper Xingu in the Brazilian Mato Grosso. Their history is inscribed in the geography of the Tuatuari and Kurisevo rivers, where their circular villages act as a materialization of their cosmology. The design of the community is not random; the so-called "path of the sun" crosses the village from east to west, dividing the space into a sacred axis that ensures that daily life unfolds in harmony with the celestial cycle.
PAGE.HERO_BODY_2: The social life of this ethnic group is defined by a radical transparency, frequently described as a circular theater where privacy is an almost non-existent concept. Inside the communal houses, the absence of walls turns every act into a shared performance, while outside, the villagers' ability to identify each member by their footprints eliminates any trace of anonymity. This forced visibility has forged a culture expert in managing public impression.
PAGE.HERO_BODY_3: Mehinaku subsistence is based on a strictly complementary sexual division of labor, where marriage constitutes the basic unit of economic survival. While men take care of fishing and clearing the jungle for cassava gardens, women assume the laborious task of processing the tuber to produce beiju, the bread that sustains life. However, this interdependence coexists with a ritualized antagonism and a policy of secrecy centered on the sacred flutes, instruments that women are forbidden to see.
PAGE.HERO_BODY_4: In their worldview, the universe is saturated with agency and inhabited by the apapaatai, powerful spirits that can bring both illness and healing. The Kwarup ritual represents the culmination of this spirituality, a moment when beautifully adorned wooden trunks personify deceased ancestors to close the cycles of mourning. Under the din of the huka-huka fight and the smoke of shamanic tobacco, the Mehinaku connect the visible world with that of the shadows.
PAGE.HERO_BODY_5: Currently, the Mehinaku face the challenges of globalization and climate change within the limits of the Xingu Indigenous Park with pragmatism. Although external deforestation and water pollution threaten vital resources like pequi and fish, the tribe has shown remarkable resilience by integrating the market economy and new technologies without sacrificing their ontological foundations. Their ability to protect their rites of passage and their ancestral language ensures that the "path of the sun" continues to guide a sovereign society.
PAGE.HERO_QUOTATION: "Where terrestrial architecture becomes a mirror of the firmament, anchoring identity to a territory sacred since mythical times."

ALDEA_SECTION.TITLE: Village Structure and Visibility
ALDEA_SECTION.DESC: The Mehinaku village, Uyapiyuku, is designed as a microcosm reflecting the architecture of the sky. Its circular layout is organized around the "path of the sun", an east-west axis connecting the Kurisevo and Tuatuari rivers. At its exact center stands the Men's House, bisecting the solar route and serving as the epicenter of public and ritual life.

TABLE.R1_C2: Axis aligning the village with the solar cycle from east to west.
TABLE.R2_C2: Central space restricted to males; the political and ritual nucleus of the community.
TABLE.R3_C2: "Often-used place": stage for speeches, ritual wrestling, and collective ceremonies.
TABLE.R4_C2: Communal structures without internal walls housing between 10 and 12 people, eliminating privacy.

DRAMA_SECTION.TITLE: Drama of Daily Life: Sociology and Behavior
DRAMA_SECTION.DESC_1: Mehinaku life is described as a "circular theater" due to the extreme visibility of individual acts. With no internal walls in the houses, and being able to recognize each neighbor's footprints, anonymity is virtually impossible. This lack of privacy has turned individuals into masters of "impression management".
DRAMA_SECTION.DESC_2: Under this system, the Mehinaku publicly project an image of generosity and exemplary citizenship while developing complex concealment strategies for their private affairs. Gossip and constant observation act as mechanisms of social control, obliging inhabitants to interpret their roles with great care to protect their status in the community.
DRAMA_SECTION.CARD1_DESC: With no walls and no anonymity, every daily act becomes a public performance before the entire village.
DRAMA_SECTION.CARD2_DESC: Individuals project generosity and virtue in public while managing concealment strategies for their private lives.
DRAMA_SECTION.CARD3_DESC: Gossip and constant observation function as ordering mechanisms that regulate the status and behavior of every member.

GENERO_SECTION.TITLE: Gender Antagonism and the Politics of Secrecy
GENERO_SECTION.DESC: Mehinaku society is governed by a "culture of exclusion" that sharply separates the domains of male and female power. The pillar of this structure is the secret of the sacred flutes, kept in the Men's House, whose sight is strictly forbidden to women under the threat of historically severe ritual sanctions.

TABLE.R1_C2: Instruments that symbolize men's political dominion; forbidden from women's sight.
TABLE.R2_C2: A foundational narrative justifying the social order by claiming women lost power in mythical time.
TABLE.R3_C2: Concept of "loss of male strength" through female sexual contamination; underpins purification rituals.
TABLE.R4_C2: Spatial division: the plaza and Men's House versus the domestic sphere and women's gardens.

GENERO_SECTION.CONCLUSION: This division generates a profound masculine sexual anxiety, where desire coexists with the fear of contamination by female fluids, reinforcing purification rituals and isolation in the Men's House.

HISTORY.TITLE:
Francisco de Orellana,
History of Amazonian exploration.
HISTORY.ORELLANA_STORY_1: In February 1542, what began as a desperate search for sustenance transformed into the most extraordinary journey ever undertaken in the New World. Francisco de Orellana, accompanied by 57 men and the friar Gaspar de Carvajal, separated from Gonzalo Pizarro’s main expedition to venture into the depths of a jungle that no one had yet charted. They were not seeking glory; they were seeking survival. Yet, destiny had reserved for them a place in eternity.
HISTORY.SUBTITLE_HUNGER: Hunger and Timber: The Birth of the "Victoria"
HISTORY.CARVAJAL_CHRONICLE: Carvajal’s chronicle, Relación del nuevo descubrimiento del famoso río Grande (Account of the Recent Discovery of the Famous Great River), recounts the sheer brutality of those early days. Weakened by famine, the men resorted to consuming the leather of their shoes and the soles of their scabbards, boiled with unknown herbs.
HISTORY.INGENUITY_VICTORIA: In a remarkable feat of ingenuity and willpower, in the heart of the wilderness, they constructed a brigantine: the San Pedro, and later, the Victoria. Without forges, without nails, and working with the damp timber of the rainforest, Orellana led an impossible engineering endeavor that would allow them to navigate the currents of a river that seemed to have no end.
HISTORY.SUBTITLE_WARRIORS: The Encounter with the Warriors: The Myth of the Amazon
HISTORY.WARRIORS_STORY: The river’s name was not born in a Spanish office, but in the heat of battle. On June 24, 1542, Carvajal recorded an encounter that would change history. The expeditionaries were attacked by a tribe led by women of great stature, fair skin, and long, braided hair, who fought with a ferocity surpassing that of any man they had ever encountered.
HISTORY.QUOTATION_WOMEN: "They fought with such intensity that it seemed each one of them was worth ten Indians," Carvajal noted.
HISTORY.NAME_BAPTISM: Inspired by the Greek myth of the Amazons, Orellana bestowed this name upon the waters he had initially called the "Rio de Orellana." Those women were real, and their resistance etched the river's name onto the map of the world forever.
HISTORY.SUBTITLE_ROUTE: From the Jungle to the Ocean: The Route
HISTORY.CAPTION_MAP: Route of nearly 5,000 kilometers followed by Francisco de Orellana through the Amazon waterway.
HISTORY.JOURNEY_DISTANCE: Over the course of seven and a half months, they traversed nearly 5,000 kilometers of waterway. They navigated through a "Freshwater Sea" where the banks would at times vanish from sight due to the sheer immensity of the flow. They endured poisoned arrows, tropical tempests, and absolute isolation.
HISTORY.END_OF_JOURNEY: Finally, on August 26, 1542, the fresh water merged with the salt of the Atlantic. Orellana and his men had crossed the continent via its wildest artery, proving that the Amazon was not merely a river, but a colossal life system connecting the Andes to the ocean.
HISTORY.LEGACY: Orellana’s expedition was not merely a territorial conquest; it was the first documented encounter with the complexity of Amazonian civilizations. Through Carvajal’s eyes, we now know that the Amazon they witnessed was not an empty wilderness, but a land inhabited by great chiefdoms and vibrant cultures that we strive to protect today.
HISTORY.FINAL_QUOTE: Orellana was not seeking the Amazon, but he had the courage not to turn his back when the river decided to claim him.

PAGE.HERO_DESC: The Amazon has been through a defining decade (2016-2026) for its survival. This biome, essential for global climate stability, now evidences an 18% cover loss, while an additional 38% suffers from some degree of degradation. This isn't just about trees disappearing, but a profound erosion of its ecological and sociocultural integrity affecting over 47 million people.
PAGE.IMAGE_CAPTION: Deforestation and fires in the Amazon basin (2024)
PAGE.SECTION_1_TITLE: The Twilight of the Jungle — A Decade of Fragmentation (2016–2026)
PAGE.BODY_1: Over the past ten years, the destructive pattern has mutated into a harder-to-track form: progressive degradation fueled by fires. While clear-cutting was historically the main concern, fire—rarely a natural occurrence in humid rainforests—now erodes biomass from the understory, weakening system resilience even if the canopy appears intact from satellites.
PAGE.BODY_2: The year 2024 became a landmark for systemic fragility. Extreme droughts, exacerbated by climate change, transformed agricultural burns into an ecological disaster impacting 4.5 million hectares of primary forest across the basin. Carbon emissions from these fires reached 791 million tons of CO₂, equaling Germany's annual footprint.
PAGE.BODY_3: The cattle ranching industry remains the dominating force, responsible for 78% of commodity-driven deforestation. With 122 million hectares already turned into pastures, this extensive model depletes soil fertility and drives economic frontiers into areas that were until recently virgin biodiversity havens.
PAGE.BODY_4: Soy expansion has introduced indirect but catastrophic pressure. In Bolivia, this phenomenon manifested brutally in 2024, seeing a 200% increase in primary forest loss driven by aggressive agricultural expansion policies feeding global grain demand.
PAGE.BODY_5: Simultaneously, mining has generated a silent contamination crisis flowing downrivers. Academic research reveals a "halo effect" where environmental impact stretches up to 70 km from official concessions. By 2026, over 2,000 sites are projected to be affected, shedding annually 4,500 tons of mercury that threaten the health of over 300 indigenous communities.
PAGE.BODY_6: Fragmentation accelerates through infrastructure like the BR-319 highway. More than 70% of historical logging occurs within a 50 km radius of paved roads. This degradation has caused the Amazon to lose its ability to "recycle" water, dangerously approaching a tipping point—situated between 20% and 25% of forest loss—after which the rainforest could collapse into an arid savanna.

PAGE.BODY_7: Facing this scenario, the last decade has also forged institutional responses of unprecedented scale. The ARPA program (Amazon Region Protected Areas) has consolidated itself as the world's largest conservation initiative, safeguarding over 62 million hectares. Its success proves that effective management and sustained financial backing can insulate ecosystems from external damage, avoiding 104 million tons of CO₂ emissions.
PAGE.BODY_8: On the ground, the JungleKeepers organization, led by Paul Rosolie and Juan Julio Durand, offers a model of direct action intertwined with deep humanity. Their strategy revolves around purchasing logging concessions prior to their destruction and transforming former loggers and miners into rangers. This approach recognizes that jungle protection entails providing dignified economic alternatives to the people dwelling at the frontiers.
PAGE.BODY_9: JungleKeepers' efforts achieved an over 90% reduction in illegal logging in their operational area within Madre de Dios, Peru. Currently protecting 135,000 acres of virgin primary rainforest, they guarantee the longevity of critical species like jaguars and harpy eagles, along with safeguarding territories of uncontacted tribes such as the Mashco Piro from outside incursions.
PAGE.BODY_10: This localized effort is complemented by the resurgence of the Amazon Fund, which in 2025 quadrupled its project approvals after a period of political inactivity. With overall footing exceeding 1.2 billion USD funding 144 projects, the fund has been a keystone for Brazil to register its lowest deforestation rate in 11 years in 2025, halting prior destructive trends.
PAGE.BODY_11: Hope also sprouts from indigenous bioeconomy, where the Xingu Seed Network shines via its regenerative impact. Involving roughly 1,000 families, the structural network has harvested 390 tons of native seeds, accelerating the restoration of 27 million trees on degraded lands. It demonstrates that ancestral know-how can effectively integrate into value chains generating community benefit without cutting down a single tree.
PAGE.BODY_12: Lastly, modern science matches indigenous wisdom: protected native territories are Earth's most efficient public health shields. A 2025 study manifested that saving these forests averts around 15 million annual cases of cardiovascular and respiratory diseases. Securing the Amazon becomes, fundamentally, an act of pervasive love and collective survival that already aligns with the blueprints and manpower needed to prevail.
